title: Former inhabitants
hook: he remembers those who lived in the woods before him, including formerly enslaved people (Walden 14)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the loon: it dived, came up somewhere else, and laughed, a man against a loon. Your line was the laughing loon. What slipped away from you, and could you enjoy the game? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-eight.

A dip in the ground in the woods, the size of a small room, softened by leaves. Stones at the edges. Nearby, a lilac bush, blooming among the trees, where no one would think to plant one. To a hiker it's scenery. To Thoreau, walking the snowy woods around Walden, a hollow like that was a cellar hole, and a lilac by it meant a doorway once stood there. Someone lived here. Someone planted that. Today, the chapter where he stops admiring the wilderness long enough to ask who was here before him.
screen: `A HOLLOW IN THE WOODS.` → `A LILAC BY IT.` → `SOMEONE LIVED HERE.`

segments.voice: First, the woods weren't empty. The chapter is called Former Inhabitants, and in it Thoreau walks the roads and hollows near his cabin and names the people who had lived there. Second, who they were. Some had been enslaved. He tells of Cato Ingraham, enslaved by a Concord gentleman, who was given a house and leave to live in Walden Woods. He tells of Zilpha, a Black woman who had a small house by the road, where she spun linen, and whose house was burned while she was away. He tells of Brister Freeman, once enslaved, who planted apple trees, and of his wife Fenda, who told fortunes, Thoreau says, pleasantly. There's a hill there still known by Brister's name, and Thoreau says he read Brister's gravestone in an old burying ground. Third, the others. He remembers poorer white neighbors too, a potter, and men who drank hard, people who lived on the edge of the town in every sense. The woods were where people went who had nowhere else. That's who his neighbors had been. Fourth, why it matters. Walden is read as a book about solitude and nature. But here, late in the book, Thoreau stops to say that the wild place he loved was full of human stories, some of them hard, and that the lilacs were still blooming for people the town might easily have forgotten. He doesn't fix that, and the chapter doesn't pretend to. He does something smaller and real. He writes their names down.
screen: `THE WOODS WEREN'T EMPTY.` · `CATO, ZILPHA, BRISTER, FENDA.` · `PEOPLE ON THE EDGE OF TOWN.` · then, large: `HE WRITES THEIR NAMES DOWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn who lived where you live. Settle, and breathe. Feel the ground under you, the floor, the building, the street. Then ask, quietly: who was here before me? The last people in this home. The people who built it. The people on this land before there were streets at all. You may not know their names. That's all right. Hold the question with respect, the way you'd stand by a cellar hole in the woods. If you pray, you can remember them in your own way. The bell holds the time.
Former inhabitants. Thoreau's chapter naming the people who lived in Walden Woods before him, among them Cato, Zilpha, Brister and Fenda. Today's word.
Your line: who was here. Today, look up one fact about the people who lived where you live, before you, and say a name out loud if you find one. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Readers of Former Inhabitants often take it as a call to remember who lived in a place before them, including people who were enslaved or poor and are seldom remembered.

fork.setup: you love these woods as wild. walking in winter, you find an old cellar hole with a lilac beside it. what does Thoreau do?
options: ignore it. it spoils the wildness.
gather the names and stories of the people who lived there.
fork.reveal: he wrote a whole chapter of names: Cato, Zilpha, Brister, Fenda, and the poor families who lived on the edge of town.

what a scholar hears: Thoreau keeps names the town might have lost, down to the gravestone he read for Brister Freeman.

notes: No direct quotations today; Thoreau's own wording uses period racial terms, and the script paraphrases. A reviewer should confirm every paraphrased detail: Cato Ingraham, enslaved by Duncan Ingraham, given a house and permission to live in Walden Woods; Zilpha, 'a colored woman', who spun linen and whose house was burned while she was away (by English soldiers on parole, in the text); Brister Freeman, 'slave of Squire Cummings once', who planted apple trees; his wife Fenda, who 'told fortunes, yet pleasantly'; Thoreau reading Brister's epitaph in the old Lincoln burying-ground; Brister's Hill.
'A potter, a drinker, an Irish laborer' summarizes Wyman the potter, Hugh Quoil and others in the chapter; confirm or trim.
'The woods were where people went who had nowhere else' is the narrator's summary of the chapter; a historian may want it softened.
'Walden is read as a book about solitude and nature' is a soft characterization of reception.
This day touches slavery in New England. It is told plainly and without drama, per the guide. A reviewer, ideally including a historian of Black New England, should read it.
